Machine learning builds models that improve from data rather than from rules you write by
hand. Over 28 lessons this course goes from fitting a straight line to training a
transformer — classical supervised methods first, then the learning theory that tells you
whether a model will generalize, then deep learning, and finally the unsupervised and
reinforcement paradigms.

Everything here runs. Every number, table, and figure on these pages was produced by
executing the code you see next to it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Start here

New to the course? Read [What Is Machine
Learning?](u01_introduction/l01_concept_intro_machine_learning.qmd), then work through
[Lab: The ML Toolkit & First
Model](u01_introduction/l02_lab_ml_toolkit_first_model.md) — it gets you training a model
in the browser within minutes, with nothing to install.
:::

## How the course works

Each lesson comes in two parts:

- **Concept notes** develop the idea and the mathematics behind an algorithm — what it
  assumes, what it optimizes, and when it fails. Start here for each lesson.
- **Labs** are runnable notebooks that implement the method and put it to work on real
  data. You open them in Google Colab and execute them yourself; every lab is paired with
  its concept note.

Classical methods use **scikit-learn**; the deep-learning unit uses **PyTorch**.

A short retrieval quiz opens most sessions, covering the previous lesson. It is low-stakes
and its purpose is to help the material stick, not to rank you.

## Course coverage

| Unit | Lessons | What you will do |
|------|---------|------------------|
| [I — Introduction](u01_introduction/l01_concept_intro_machine_learning.qmd) | L01–L02 | What machine learning is and when it is the right tool; the toolkit, and your first trained model end to end |
| [II — Supervised Learning](u02_supervised_learning/l03_concept_linear_regression.qmd) | L03–L08 | Linear and logistic regression; linear classifiers; Gaussian discriminant analysis; naive Bayes; support vector machines |
| [III — Learning Theory](u03_learning_theory/l09_concept_bias_variance_cv.qmd) | L09–L11 | The bias–variance dilemma and cross-validation; regularization and model selection; the evaluation metrics that decide whether a model is actually good |
| [IV — Ensembles](u04_ensembles/l12_concept_trees_bagging.qmd) | L12–L13 | Decision trees and bagging; boosting — turning weak learners into a strong one |
| [V — Deep Learning](u05_deep_learning/l14_concept_perceptron_neural_networks.qmd) | L14–L22 | Perceptrons to multilayer networks; backpropagation and autodiff; training deep networks; CNNs on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10; transfer learning; autoencoders; attention and the Transformer |
| [VI — Unsupervised Learning](u06_unsupervised_learning/l23_concept_kmeans_clustering.qmd) | L23–L25 | Similarity and k-means; hierarchical and density-based clustering; Gaussian mixtures and the EM algorithm |
| [VII — Dimensionality Reduction](u07_dimensionality_reduction/l26_concept_pca.qmd) | L26–L27 | Principal component analysis; factor analysis and independent component analysis |
| [VIII — Reinforcement Learning](u08_reinforcement_learning/l28_concept_reinforcement_learning.qmd) | L28 | The reinforcement-learning paradigm — agents, states, rewards, and how it differs from everything before it |

## Running the labs

Labs are Jupyter notebooks designed to run in **Google Colab** — free, in the browser,
nothing to install, and a GPU available for the deep-learning lessons. Every lab page
carries an *Open in Colab* badge at the top; click it and the notebook opens ready to run.

A few things worth knowing:

- **Run the setup cells first.** Each lab opens with two of them: one installs the
  libraries, one imports them and loads the data. Colab resets between sessions, so run
  them every time you open a lab.
- **Save your own copy.** Clicking the badge opens a read-only view of the course
  notebook. Use *File · Save a copy in Drive* before you start working, or your edits are
  lost when you close the tab.
- **The data comes with the lab.** Datasets are bundled or downloaded by the setup cell,
  so labs work without hunting for files.
- **The lab pages on this site are read-only.** They show the code together with the
  output it actually produced — useful for reading and review, but you learn this by
  running it yourself.

## What you will be able to do

By the end of the course you should be able to:

1. Decide which machine-learning approach fits a given problem.
2. Preprocess and integrate heterogeneous data sources into input a learning algorithm can
   use directly.
3. Write efficient code applying the main machine-learning algorithms to specific problems.
4. Evaluate a model's performance against the criteria of learning theory — not just its
   accuracy on the data it was trained on.
5. Apply recent and specialized deep-learning algorithms, up to and including the
   architecture behind modern language models.

## How you are assessed

| | |
|---|---|
| **Retrieval quizzes** | Short multiple-choice, at the start of most sessions, on the previous lesson |
| **Assignments** | One per major unit (II, III/IV, V), autograded |
| **Partial exams** | Exam I after Unit IV — classical supervised learning, learning theory, ensembles; Exam II after Unit V — deep learning |
| **Final project** | Assigned around week 8, presented during finals week; it is also how Units VI–VIII are assessed |

Relative weights are discussed and agreed on the first day of class.
